ideas.hypothesis: Following endogenous growth theory, a shift of the public expenditure structure toward productive (education, health, infrastructure) and away from maintenance/administrative spending raises per-capita growth, and the effect works through crowding in private investment, so the growth effect is larger where private investment responds positively to public capital spending.

sources.role: finding: social expenditures (education, health) raise growth in OECD panel
finding/measure: classification into social, economic and maintaining expenditures with different growth signs
mechanism: crowding-in vs crowding-out of private expenditure
method: VECM and impulse responses for debt-financed development spending and private investment

ideas.test: Panel of 30-50 countries, 1995-2019, using IMF COFOG functional spending shares; regress 5-year average per-capita growth on productive-spending share (holding total spending constant) with system GMM, and add an interaction with an estimated country-specific private-investment response to public capital spending (from country VARs).
ideas.disconfirming: The productive-spending share has no positive association with growth after controlling for total spending, or the effect is equally large where public spending crowds out private investment.

ideas.hypothesis: Estimated beta-convergence speed is systematically larger when growth determinants (investment, openness, life expectancy, schooling) are included and allowed heterogeneous slopes, so that cross-region differences in unconditional convergence speed (e.g. ASEAN vs Latin America) are largely explained by differences in steady-state determinants rather than by integration per se.

sources.role: method/finding: PMG estimator and wide range of convergence speeds in ASEAN5
finding: conditional convergence in Latin America with Barro-style determinants
setting: beta convergence in EU regional labour market indicators

ideas.test: Penn World Table data for ASEAN and Latin American countries 1960-2019; estimate unconditional and conditional beta with both pooled fixed-effects and PMG; compare how much the regional gap in convergence speed shrinks once determinants are added.
ideas.disconfirming: Adding determinants leaves the regional gap in convergence speed unchanged, or conditional and unconditional speeds are statistically identical.

ideas.hypothesis: Sigma convergence (falling dispersion of income) occurs only in country groups where the dispersion of key growth determinants (investment rates, life expectancy, openness) also falls, so the trend in determinant dispersion predicts the trend in income dispersion.

sources.role: finding: beta and sigma convergence after ASEAN expansion
measure: Barro-Sala-i-Martin determinants for Latin America
finding: convergence reversed to divergence in 2008-2009 in EU regions

ideas.test: Compute rolling standard deviation of log GDP per capita and of each determinant for ASEAN, Latin America and EU groups 1960-2019; test co-movement with regressions of change in income dispersion on change in determinant dispersion.
ideas.disconfirming: Income dispersion falls while determinant dispersion rises or stays flat, or the two series are unrelated.

ideas.hypothesis: Domestic basic research stock raises the absorptive capacity for foreign R&D spillovers, so the TFP contribution of trade-embodied foreign R&D is larger in regions or periods with a higher basic-research share of R&D.

sources.role: mechanism: fundamental vs secondary knowledge drives path-dependent innovation
method/measure: Coe-Helpman spillover model and TFP decomposition for China

ideas.test: Chinese provincial panel 2000-2019: TFP growth regressed on domestic R&D stock, import-weighted foreign R&D stock, and its interaction with the province's basic-research share of R&D expenditure (from statistical yearbooks of science and technology).
ideas.disconfirming: The interaction term is zero or negative.

ideas.hypothesis: Knowledge stock only promotes innovation and growth when the basic-research share of R&D is above a threshold, explaining why aggregate knowledge stock appears insignificant in Chinese provincial data.

sources.role: mechanism: basic vs applied research allocation in endogenous growth model
finding: knowledge stock insignificant for innovation in China; Feder-type spillover measure
setting/method: endogenous growth model estimated on provincial panel

ideas.test: Chinese provincial panel 2008-2019 with patents and GDP growth as outcomes; threshold panel regression of outcome on knowledge stock with basic-research share as the threshold variable.
ideas.disconfirming: No threshold is found, or knowledge stock is insignificant in both regimes.

ideas.hypothesis: Tests of Wagner's law in transition economies are sensitive to how growth is measured: using catch-up-adjusted (PPP and convergence-adjusted) growth instead of raw real GDP growth weakens the estimated growth-to-spending causality.

sources.role: measure: catch-up-adjusted growth measurement in Central Caucaso-Asia
method/finding: panel tests of Wagner vs Keynes in South Caucasus

ideas.test: Panel of the 8 Central Caucaso-Asian countries 1995-2019; run panel Granger causality between real government expenditure and (i) raw real GDP and (ii) catch-up-adjusted GDP; compare coefficients.
ideas.disconfirming: Wagner-type causality is equally strong under both growth measures.

ideas.hypothesis: The bidirectional causality between government spending and GDP found in South Caucasus panels partly reflects common catch-up dynamics; after removing the catch-up component from growth, causality becomes one-directional.

sources.role: finding: mutual causality between spending and GDP
measure: adjustment of growth for catch-up effect

ideas.test: Same South Caucasus panel 1995-2019; estimate panel VAR with raw and catch-up-detrended GDP, using Dumitrescu-Hurlin causality tests.
ideas.disconfirming: Bidirectional causality persists after the catch-up adjustment.

ideas.hypothesis: Imports of capital and intermediate goods, not total imports, Granger-cause GDP growth in China; studies that find no import-led growth use aggregate imports that mix consumer goods.

sources.role: finding: imports promote growth in China 1978-2007
finding: imports have net negative direct effect offset via consumption
finding/method: Shenzhen cointegration and ECM showing GDP causes trade

ideas.test: Chinese national and provincial data 1990-2019 with imports split by BEC category; VECM and Granger causality for each import type versus GDP.
ideas.disconfirming: Capital/intermediate imports do not Granger-cause GDP, or behave no differently from consumer imports.

ideas.hypothesis: Primary enrolment raises growth mainly indirectly by enabling secondary enrolment and ICT diffusion, so primary enrolment loses its effect once secondary enrolment and internet penetration are controlled.

sources.role: finding: secondary enrolment matters more than nutrition for growth
mechanism: educational attainment levels linked to ICT diffusion

ideas.test: Cross-country panel 1990-2019 (World Bank WDI): mediation analysis of 5-year growth on lagged primary enrolment with secondary enrolment and internet users as mediators.
ideas.disconfirming: Primary enrolment retains a large direct effect after mediators are included.

ideas.hypothesis: In Kyrgyzstan and comparable CIS economies, faster growth lowers external debt ratios, but the effect is weaker than in South American young democracies because of dependence on remittances and external financing.

sources.role: finding/method: growth reduces debt ratios, dynamic panel
setting: monetary and external debt indicators for Kyrgyzstan and CIS
setting: transition economy panel methods
setting: Central Asian growth measurement

ideas.test: Panel of CIS countries 2000-2019 with external debt/GDP, growth, remittances; dynamic panel (PMG) comparing growth coefficient against a South American benchmark sample.
ideas.disconfirming: Growth has no effect on debt ratios in CIS countries, or the effect equals the South American one.
